questions.q: In a Windows file search, the pattern *report*.xlsx will find:
options: All .xlsx files whose names contain the word report
All files of any type containing report
questions.solution: The asterisk matches any number of characters, so *report*.xlsx matches any Excel workbook with 'report' anywhere in its name - e.g. annual-report-2026.xlsx and report-final.xlsx.
questions.shortcut: Prefix * = anything before, suffix * = anything after; .xlsx at the end restricts the type.

questions.q: The superscript formatting shortcut in MS Word is:
questions.solution: Ctrl+Shift+= applies superscript (x squared style); Ctrl+= applies subscript (H2O style). Ctrl+Shift+S opens the Apply Styles box.
questions.shortcut: Shift pushes the number UP: Shift with = gives the raised (super) script.

questions.q: In Chrome and Edge, which shortcut opens the 'Clear browsing data' dialog?
questions.solution: Ctrl+Shift+Delete opens the dialog for clearing history, cookies and cached files. Shift+Delete is permanent file deletion in File Explorer, not a browser command.
questions.shortcut: Ctrl+Shift = the strong version; the strongest delete wipes browsing data.

questions.q: The keyboard shortcut to insert the current date into a cell (as a fixed value) is:
questions.solution: Ctrl+; stamps today's date; Ctrl+Shift+; stamps the time; Ctrl+D fills down from the cell above; Ctrl+T creates a table.
questions.shortcut: Semicolon = stamp. Shift makes it time instead of date.

questions.q: Select the correct passive form of the sentence: 'The students have cleaned the auditorium.'
options: The auditorium have been cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has being cleaned by the students.
The auditorium is cleaned by the students.
The auditorium has been cleaned by the students.
questions.solution: Present perfect row → **has/have been + V3**; the new subject *the auditorium* is singular, so **has been cleaned by the students**. 'Have been cleaned' agrees with the old subject; 'has being cleaned' puts being in a perfect slot; 'is cleaned' switches to the simple present row.
questions.shortcut: Perfect active → has/have been + V3. Agree with the NEW subject.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

Each of the shortlisted candidates **are** to report by nine tomorrow.
questions.solution: **Each** is unconditionally singular → each **is** to report. The plural *candidates* inside the 'of' phrase cannot change the opener.

questions.q: What is the main point of the second paragraph?
options: Any family member, in any language, can give a child the benefits of stories
Reading aloud helps only when parents are highly educated
Folk tales are more useful than newspapers
Children learn best from their older sisters
questions.solution: P2's topic sentence: 'The effect does not depend on expensive books or educated parents.' The three examples (grandmother in Bhojpuri, father with a newspaper, sister acting a story) all give 'the same things'. So anyone, in any language, can help. The second option reverses the topic sentence; the last two pick one example and rank it, which the passage never does.
questions.shortcut: When a paragraph lists several examples that 'all give the same things', its point is what they share.
questions.passage:
Parents often wait for school to teach their children to read. Yet research on early learning keeps pointing to what happens before school begins. Children who are read to at home, even for fifteen minutes a day, arrive in class knowing more words, listening for longer and treating books as a pleasure rather than a task.

The effect does not depend on expensive books or educated parents. A grandmother telling a folk tale in Bhojpuri, a father reading the Sunday newspaper aloud, an older sister acting out a story with funny voices — each gives the child the same things: new words, the rhythm of sentences and the habit of paying attention.

Busy families may feel they have no time to spare. But fifteen minutes is shorter than most television serials. If every home set aside that small window each evening, schools would receive children who are ready not just to read, but to want to read.

questions.q:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.

The road is being repaired by the workers.
options: The workers is repairing the road.
The workers have repaired the road.
The workers are repairing the road.
The workers are repaired the road.
questions.solution: 'is being + V3' → present continuous: **are repairing** (plural subject). B writes V3 after are; C fails number; D changes tense to perfect.

questions.q: The main constituent of CNG (compressed natural gas) is:
questions.solution: CNG is mostly **methane**. LPG is mainly **butane** with propane.

questions.q: The **Subsidiary Alliance** system was introduced by —
questions.solution: **Lord Wellesley** (1798–1805) made Indian rulers keep British troops at their own cost and accept a British Resident; the Nizam of Hyderabad signed first (1798).

questions.q: The Telugu work ***Amuktamalyada*** was written by which Vijayanagara ruler?
questions.solution: **Krishnadevaraya** (Tuluva dynasty) wrote *Amuktamalyada*, about the Alvar saint Andal. His court had the eight poets called **Ashtadiggajas**.

questions.q: The writ of 'quo warranto' is issued to:
options: release a person from illegal detention
direct a public official to perform his duty
question the legality of a person holding a public office
quash the order of a lower court
questions.solution: **Quo warranto** literally means 'by what authority' — it prevents a person from unlawfully occupying a public office. Release from illegal detention is *habeas corpus*; commanding performance of duty is *mandamus*; quashing a lower court's order is *certiorari*.
questions.shortcut: warranto ~ 'where is your warrant to hold this post?'

questions.q: A is 3 times as efficient as B, and together they finish a work in 12 days. A alone will finish it in:
Ravi saves 25% of his income. His income rises by 30% and his expenditure rises by 20%. His new savings are what per cent more than his earlier savings?
questions.solution:
Income = 100 → saves 25, spends 75.
New: income 130, expenditure 90 → savings 40.
Increase $= \frac{15}{25} \times 100 = 60\%$.

questions.q: The HCF of 0.54, 1.8 and 7.2 is:
questions.solution:
Write all with two decimal places: 0.54, 1.80, 7.20.
$\gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18$ ⇒ HCF $= 0.18$.
questions.shortcut: Clear decimals (×100): gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18, shift the point back → 0.18.

questions.q: Two numbers, when divided by 17, leave remainders 13 and 11 respectively. What is the remainder when their product is divided by 17?

Three of the following four letter-clusters are alike in a certain way and one is different. Find the odd one out. (The letters follow English alphabetical order.)

**NOP, HIJ, DEF, RST**
questions.solution: All four have steps (+1, +1), so steps cannot decide. NOP, HIJ and DEF have a **vowel in the middle** (O, I, E). RST has no vowel → **RST**.

questions.shortcut: Sum, subtract pairs, re-add the triple.

questions.q: **Anil is the brother of Sunil. Sunil is the father of Mohan. Ritu is the daughter of Kavita. Mohan is the brother of Ritu.** How is **Kavita related to Anil**?
questions.solution: Mohan and Ritu share parents; Ritu's mother is Kavita, so Kavita is Sunil's wife. Wife of Anil's brother → Anil's **sister-in-law**. (Aunt would need Kavita on the parents' generation of Anil — she is on Anil's own row.)
questions.shortcut: Rebuild top-down: the shared-parent sentence joins the scattered names.

questions.q: Find the odd one out: **River, Pond, Lake, Sea**
questions.solution: River, pond and lake are **freshwater** bodies; the sea is **saline** → **Sea**.
questions.shortcut: Water bodies split on salinity first, then on flow (flowing vs still).
questions.pattern: word odd one out — category break
